lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- The Team You Built
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flavio Gattaz | Lesson 17 -- The Team You Built
lesson.grammar_point: cause and consequence (because of vs because, due to, as a result, which is why, lead to, result in, result from)

listenings.text: When I ask a candidate about a team he built, most people give me an organization chart. Twelve engineers, three foremen, one assistant. That tells me the size of the team, and nothing else. What I am really listening for is cause and consequence. Why did you hire this person and not that one? What happened as a result? A strong answer connects every decision to what it led to. The second thing I listen for is the people who left. Every real team loses somebody, and staff turnover is a normal part of building anything. If a candidate tells me that nobody ever left his team, I do not believe him, or I suspect that he never asked anybody to change. The third thing is simple. I want to hear one person by name, somebody you hired or promoted, and what that person is doing today. Because of that one detail, I can usually tell whether you built the team, or only inherited it.

Early in my career I made a hire I was very proud of. I poached a brilliant engineer from our biggest competitor, and I paid him almost twice what my other engineers earned. On paper he had the perfect skill set. In practice he was not a cultural fit. He made every decision alone, and he never explained anything to the younger engineers. As a result, two of them resigned in the same month, and the team lost more knowledge than he had brought in. The problem was not really him. It was the reason I hired him. I had looked only at his technical record, and not at all at how he worked with people. Since then, every candidate for a senior role spends a full day on one of our sites with the team before we make an offer. It takes longer, and we lose some good people because of it. But in the last five years we have not had to replace a single senior hire.
